Ufton Nervet. To the S. of Theale. Spelt Uftone, F.A. (1316). Even without other forms to guide us, it is obvious that the A.S. form must have been UfFantun, i. e. The form nervet is the exact Norman equivalent of the Old French nerve, which Gode- froy explains as ' full of nerve, strong ' ; so that it was originally a complimentary epithet.

There are about thirty Westons. Woolhampton. Between Thatcham and Theale (nearly). I discuss the suffix -Hampton at p. 102. In this case the old form did not really possess that suffix, as will appear. Spelt Wullaminton, H.R. ; Wolamptone, F.A. (1428) ; Wllaumton, R.T. But earlier, it is Wulavinton, T.N. ; Wullavintoii, R.C. D.B. has OUavintone, p. 10 ; with 0 for Wu. It thus appears that the successive forms were Wullavintoii, Wullaminton, Wollamton, Wolhampton, &c. The form Wullavintoii fairly agrees with the modern names Woolavington, Somersets., and Woollavington, Sussex. All have the same origin ; and as the A.S. f between two vowels denotes v, we find the same prefix as in the A.S. Wullafing- land, which occurs in Kemble, Cod. Dipl. vi. 243. Further, Wullaf is a late form of Wulflaf, due to assimilation. Hence the A.S. form of Woolhamp- ton must originally have been Wulflafinga-tun, i.e. ' town (or farm) of the Wulfiafings or sons of Wulflaf '. Wulflaf (later Wullaf) is a known name.
